title: The code roll
story: Bit rolls through a heavy door into the Archive: rows of dusty terminals, each one humming with old records. The first terminal holds a roll of door codes. WARDEN locked the next two doors with the first and the last code on that roll, and the roll is a different length every night.
power: A list keeps many values together, in order, under one name. You write it with square brackets [ ], the items separated by commas. When Bit scans a terminal, it often gets a list back. ### Reading items by index Each item has an index: its position in the list. Counting starts at 0, just like the characters of a string. A negative index counts from the end: -1 is the last item, -2 the one before it. len(list) gives the number of items. ~~~python codes = [4417, 2093, 8851, 1270] print(codes) print(codes[0]) print(codes[1]) print(codes[-1]) print(len(codes)) ~~~ - Line 1: codes holds a list of 4 numbers. - Line 2: prints the whole list: [4417, 2093, 8851, 1270]. - Line 3: index 0 is the first item: 4417. - Line 4: index 1 is the second item: 2093. - Line 5: index -1 is the last item: 1270, however long the list is. - Line 6: 4 items, so 4. ### Slicing: a piece of a list lst[a:b] is a slice: a new list with the items from index a up to, but not including, index b. Leave a side empty to start at the beginning or go to the end. Negative indexes work in slices too, so codes[1:-1] is everything except the first and the last item. The original list does not change. ~~~python codes = [4417, 2093, 8851, 1270] print(codes[0:2]) print(codes[:3]) print(codes[2:]) print(codes[1:-1]) print(codes) ~~~ - Line 2: indexes 0 and 1: [4417, 2093]. - Line 3: from the start up to index 3 (not included): [4417, 2093, 8851]. - Line 4: from index 2 to the end: [8851, 1270]. - Line 5: without the first and the last: [2093, 8851]. - Line 6: the list itself is unchanged. ### Looping over a list A for loop over a list gives you each item in turn, from index 0 to the end. ~~~python codes = [4417, 2093, 8851] for c in codes: print("trying", c) print("done,", len(codes), "codes tried") ~~~ ### Common mistakes - Using index 1 for the first item. The first item is index 0. - Using codes[len(codes)] for the last item: that index is one past the end and stops the program with an IndexError. Use codes[-1]. - Forgetting that the end of a slice is not included.
goal: Scan the terminal, unlock door A with the first code and door B with the last code, and reach the exit. Then say Codes: and how many codes the roll has, and Unused: followed by the slice of codes between the first and the last.
starter:
from robot import *

move()
codes = scan()
# codes is a list. Door A is right in front of you.
solution:
from robot import *

move()
codes = scan()
unlock(codes[0])
move()
move()
unlock(codes[-1])
move()
move()
say("Codes:", len(codes))
say("Unused:", codes[1:-1])
hint: The first item is codes[0], the last is codes[-1], and codes[1:-1] is everything in between.

title: The furnace log
story: The next terminal keeps the furnace temperature log, one reading per hour. WARDEN set the doors to clever codes: door A wants the spread of the readings (the biggest minus the smallest), door B wants their average. Get one number wrong and the alarm goes off.
power: Some functions take a list and answer a question about it, without changing the list. ### Asking questions about a list - sum(list) adds all the numbers. - max(list) and min(list) give the biggest and the smallest item. - sorted(list) gives a new list in increasing order. sorted(list, reverse=True) gives decreasing order. The reverse=True part is a named argument: an option given by its name. - x in list gives True if x is one of the items, otherwise False. ~~~python temps = [62, 48, 75, 51] print(sum(temps)) print(max(temps), min(temps)) print(sorted(temps)) print(sorted(temps, reverse=True)) print(75 in temps, 99 in temps) print(temps) ~~~ - Line 2: 62 + 48 + 75 + 51: prints 236. - Line 3: prints 75 48. - Line 4: prints [48, 51, 62, 75]. - Line 5: prints [75, 62, 51, 48]. - Line 6: prints True False. - Line 7: the original list is unchanged: [62, 48, 75, 51]. ### The average An average is the total divided by how many values there are: sum(list) / len(list). The division gives a float, often with many decimals, so wrap it in round(..., 1) to keep one decimal. Python computes the innermost parentheses first. ~~~python temps = [62, 48, 75, 51] average = sum(temps) / len(temps) print(average) print(round(average, 1)) print(round(sum([3, 4, 4]) / 3, 1)) ~~~ - Line 2: 236 divided by 4: average gets 59.0. - Line 4: already one decimal: 59.0. - Line 5: 11 divided by 3 is 3.666..., rounded to 3.7. ### Building a new list with a loop To keep only some items, start with an empty list [], loop over the original list, and .append the items that pass an if test. .append(x) adds x at the end of a list. The new list keeps the original order. ~~~python temps = [62, 48, 75, 51] hot = [] for t in temps: if t > 60: hot.append(t) print("checked", t, "hot is now", hot) print(hot) ~~~ - Line 2: hot starts empty. - Round 1: 62 is above 60, so hot becomes [62]. Round 2: 48 is skipped. Round 3: 75 is added. Round 4: 51 is skipped. - Line 7 prints [62, 75]. ### Common mistakes - Writing hot = hot.append(t). append changes the list and returns nothing, so this replaces your list with None. Just write hot.append(t). - Creating the empty list inside the loop, which empties it on every round. - Confusing "strictly above" (>) with "above or equal" (>=). - Forgetting round when a number of decimals is asked.
goal: Scan the log. Unlock door A with the biggest reading minus the smallest, and door B with the average rounded to 1 decimal. At the exit, say Hot: and the list of readings strictly above 50 (in log order), then Top three: and the three highest readings, highest first.
starter:
from robot import *

move()
temps = scan()
move()
solution:
from robot import *

move()
temps = scan()
move()
unlock(max(temps) - min(temps))
move()
move()
unlock(round(sum(temps) / len(temps), 1))
hot = []
for t in temps:
    if t > 50:
        hot.append(t)
move()
move()
move()
say("Hot:", hot)
say("Top three:", sorted(temps, reverse=True)[:3])
hint: round(sum(temps) / len(temps), 1) is the average, and a slice [:3] of the list sorted with reverse=True gives the top three.

title: The scrambled route card
story: Behind the doors, the Archive turns into a maze of shelves. A terminal gives Bit the route through it as a list of steps, but WARDEN has scrambled the card: useless static steps are mixed in, and one extra move was added at the very end. That last step walks straight into a pit.
power: Unlike a string, a list can be changed in place. That is how Bit cleans a damaged list before using it. ### Changing a list These methods (functions attached to a value, called with a dot) change the list itself: - .append(x) adds x at the end. - .insert(i, x) puts x at index i, moving the others one place to the right. - .remove(x) deletes the first item equal to x. - .pop() removes the last item and gives it back to you. ~~~python steps = ["move", "left"] steps.append("move") print(steps) steps.insert(0, "right") print(steps) steps.remove("left") print(steps) last = steps.pop() print(last, steps) ~~~ - Line 2: steps becomes ['move', 'left', 'move']. Line 3 prints it. - Line 4: "right" goes to index 0: ['right', 'move', 'left', 'move']. - Line 6: the first "left" is removed: ['right', 'move', 'move']. - Line 8: the last item is taken out and stored in last. - Line 9: prints move ['right', 'move']. ### Removing every copy of a value .remove only deletes the first copy, and it stops the program with a ValueError if the value is not there. Combine it with in and a while loop to delete every copy safely. ~~~python card = ["move", "static", "left", "static", "move"] while "static" in card: card.remove("static") print(card) print(len(card), "real steps") ~~~ ### Following a list of instructions A for loop over the list, with an if / elif chain inside, turns each word into an action. ~~~python card = ["move", "move", "left", "move"] for step in card: if step == "move": print("going forward") elif step == "left": print("turning left") else: print("turning right") ~~~ ### Common mistakes - Calling .remove(x) when x is not in the list: ValueError. Check with in first. - Writing card = card.pop(): now card is the removed item, not the list. - Changing a list while a for loop runs over that same list: items get skipped. Clean it first, then loop.
goal: Scan the route card, throw away its last step with pop(), remove every static step, and say Clean route: followed by the number of steps left and the word steps. Then follow the clean route (move, left or right) to the exit.
starter:
from robot import *

move()
route = scan()
# clean the route, then follow it
hint: Pop first, then use while "static" in route: route.remove("static") before the for loop that drives Bit.

title: The key cabinet
story: Two terminals stand side by side at the end of the shelves. The first is WARDEN's key cabinet: every door letter with its code. The second is the night patch: codes WARDEN changed since the cabinet was printed. Use an old code and the doors stay shut.
power: A dictionary, or dict, stores pairs: a key and its value. Think of a phone book (name to number). You look things up by key instead of by position, and it is instant. ### Creating a dict and looking up a key A dict is written with curly braces { }. Inside, each pair is key: value, and pairs are separated by commas. To read a value, put its key in square brackets. len counts the pairs. ~~~python cabinet = {"A": 4417, "B": 2093, "lamp": "off"} print(cabinet) print(cabinet["B"]) print(len(cabinet)) ~~~ - Line 1: "A" is a key, 4417 is its value. Values can be of any kind. - Line 3: looks up the key "B" and prints 2093. - Line 4: 3 pairs, so 3. ### Adding and updating Assigning to a key adds the pair if the key is new, or replaces the value if the key already exists. A dict never holds the same key twice. ~~~python stock = {"bolt": 5} stock["gear"] = 3 stock["bolt"] = 10 stock["bolt"] = stock["bolt"] + 1 print(stock) ~~~ - Line 2: "gear" is new, so it is added. - Line 3: "bolt" exists, so its value is replaced by 10. - Line 4: reads 10, adds 1, stores 11. - Line 5: prints {'bolt': 11, 'gear': 3}. ### Missing keys: in and .get Reading a key that does not exist with square brackets stops the program with a KeyError. Two safe tools: key in d tells you if the key exists, and d.get(key, default) gives the value, or the default when the key is missing. ~~~python cabinet = {"A": 4417} print("A" in cabinet, "C" in cabinet) print(cabinet.get("A", "none")) print(cabinet.get("C", "none")) ~~~ - Line 2: prints True False. - Line 3: the key exists: 4417. - Line 4: "C" is missing, so the default is returned: none. ### Looping over a dict A for loop over a dict gives you its keys. .items() gives the pairs, and you can receive each pair into two loop variables at once: for key, value in d.items():. .keys() gives only the keys and .values() only the values. ~~~python patch = {"B": 7719, "C": 5150} for door in patch: print(door) for door, code in patch.items(): print(f"door {door} now uses {code}") print(list(patch.keys()), list(patch.values())) ~~~ - Lines 2 and 3: door gets "B", then "C". - Lines 4 and 5: on round 1, door is "B" and code is 7719. - Line 6: prints ['B', 'C'] [7719, 5150]. list(...) turns them into plain lists. ### Common mistakes - Reading a missing key with d[key]: KeyError. Use d.get(key, default) or check with in. - Forgetting the quotes around text keys: cabinet[A] looks for a variable called A.
goal: Scan the cabinet (terminal 1) and the patch (terminal 2). Copy every pair of the patch into the cabinet, then unlock doors A and B with the up-to-date codes and reach the exit. Finally say Spare code for C: and the code of door C, or none if the cabinet has no key C.
starter:
from robot import *

move()
cabinet = scan()
move()
patch = scan()
solution:
from robot import *

move()
cabinet = scan()
move()
patch = scan()
for door, code in patch.items():
    cabinet[door] = code
unlock(cabinet["A"])
move()
unlock(cabinet["B"])
move()
move()
move()
say("Spare code for C:", cabinet.get("C", "none"))
hint: Loop over patch.items() and assign cabinet[door] = code; cabinet.get("C", "none") handles the missing key.

title: The parts tally
story: A terminal prints the parts list of the last shift as one long line of words. WARDEN's riddle on the door reads: the password is the part used most often. Bit has to count every part, then shout the tally so the radio log keeps a copy.
power: The classic job of a dict is counting. ### Counting things Start with an empty dict {}. For each item, take its current count with .get(item, 0) (0 the first time you see it), add 1, and store it back. To count the words of a text, loop over text.split(), which cuts the text at the spaces into a list of words. ~~~python counts = {} for part in "gear bolt gear nut gear".split(): counts[part] = counts.get(part, 0) + 1 print(part, counts) ~~~ - Round 1: "gear" is missing, .get gives 0, so counts["gear"] becomes 1. - Round 2: "bolt" becomes 1. Round 3: "gear" becomes 2. - It ends as {'gear': 3, 'bolt': 1, 'nut': 1}. Keys stay in the order they were first added. ### Finding the key with the biggest value max(d) alone compares the keys themselves (alphabetically for text). The named argument key= tells max what to compare instead. With key=d.get, it compares d.get(k) for each key k, which is the value, and still returns the key. d.get has no parentheses here: you hand over the method itself, and max calls it. ~~~python counts = {"gear": 3, "bolt": 1, "nut": 1} print(max(counts)) best = max(counts, key=counts.get) print(best) for part, n in counts.items(): print(part, n) ~~~ - Line 2: compares the keys as text: nut is last alphabetically, so it prints nut. Wrong answer. - Line 3: compares the values 3, 1 and 1 and returns the key of the biggest: gear. - Lines 5 and 6: print the tally, one pair per line. ### Common mistakes - Writing counts[part] = counts[part] + 1: the first time, the key is missing and you get a KeyError. - Writing key=counts.get() with parentheses inside max. - Using max(counts) without key=, which compares the names, not the counts.
goal: Scan the parts line, count each part into a dict called counts, and unlock door A with the most frequent part. At the exit, say each part and its count, one per line (like gear 3), in the order the parts first appear.
starter:
from robot import *

move()
line = scan()
counts = {}
solution:
from robot import *

move()
line = scan()
counts = {}
for part in line.split():
    counts[part] = counts.get(part, 0) + 1
unlock(max(counts, key=counts.get))
move()
move()
for part, n in counts.items():
    say(part, n)
hint: counts[part] = counts.get(part, 0) + 1 inside a loop over line.split(), then max(counts, key=counts.get).
test: assert isinstance(counts, dict) and len(counts) > 0, 'Count the parts into a dict called counts.'

title: The badge camera
story: The Archive's last door is watched by a camera that logs every badge it sees, again and again. A second terminal lists the badges allowed in this wing. Door A opens for the number of different badges the camera saw, and Bit must report every intruder before slipping out.
power: Two more ways to group values. A tuple is a fixed record that cannot change, like a position on a map. A set keeps each value only once, which is perfect for removing duplicates. ### Tuples: fixed groups of values A tuple is written with round brackets, the items separated by commas. You read items by index like a list, but you cannot add, remove or replace anything. Bit's own position() sensor returns a tuple (x, y). ~~~python point = (3, 4) print(point) print(point[0], point[1]) print(len(point)) ~~~ - Line 2: prints (3, 4). - Line 3: index 0 is 3, index 1 is 4. - Line 4: prints 2. ### Unpacking You can put each item of a tuple (or a list) into its own variable in one line. The number of names on the left must match the number of items. This is what for k, v in d.items() was already doing. .split("@") cuts a text at the @ character instead of at spaces, and the pieces unpack nicely. ~~~python point = (3, 4) x, y = point print("x is", x, "and y is", y) user, domain = "ana@ironworks.com".split("@") print(user, domain) print("ana@ironworks.com".split("@")[1]) ~~~ - Line 2: x gets 3 and y gets 4. - Line 4: the split gives ['ana', 'ironworks.com'], so user gets "ana" and domain gets "ironworks.com". - Line 6: without unpacking, index 1 of the split gives the part after the @ directly. ### Sets: unique values A set is written with curly braces, like a dict but with single values instead of pairs. It keeps each value once and has no order, so it has no index. set(a_list) turns a list into a set, removing duplicates. An empty set is written set(), because {} means an empty dict. in works on sets and is very fast. ~~~python numbers = [3, 1, 3, 2, 1, 3] unique = set(numbers) print(unique) print(len(numbers), len(unique)) print(2 in unique) ~~~ - Line 2: unique gets {1, 2, 3}. - Line 4: prints 6 3: six items in the list, three distinct. - Line 5: prints True. ### Adding to a set, and sorting it .add(x) puts a value into a set; adding a value already there does nothing. A set of text can print in a different order from one run to the next, so use sorted(a_set), which returns a new list in a fixed order. ~~~python badges = set() for b in ["K22", "B17", "K22", "Z09"]: badges.add(b) print(len(badges), "distinct so far") result = sorted(badges) print(result) print(type(result)) ~~~ - Round 3: "K22" is already there, so the count stays 2. - Line 6: prints ['B17', 'K22', 'Z09']. - Line 7: prints <class 'list'>: sorted always gives a list. ### Combining sets | (union) gives everything in either set, & (intersection) gives what is in both, - (difference) gives what is in the first but not the second. ~~~python a = {1, 2, 3} b = {2, 3, 4} print(a | b) print(a & b) print(a - b) ~~~ - Prints {1, 2, 3, 4}, then {2, 3}, then {1}. ### Common mistakes - Writing {} for an empty set: that is an empty dict. Use set(). - Trying my_set[0]: sets have no positions. - Expecting a set to print in a fixed order. Use sorted(). - Using .append on a set. Sets use .add. - Trying to change a tuple, like point[0] = 5: tuples cannot change.
goal: Scan the camera log (terminal 1) and the allowed list (terminal 2). Unlock door A with the number of distinct badges seen. Say Intruders: with the sorted list of badges seen but not allowed, and Cleared: with the sorted list of badges both seen and allowed. Walk to the exit, then unpack position() and say Out at x, the x value, y, the y value.
starter:
from robot import *

move()
seen = scan()
solution:
from robot import *

move()
seen = scan()
move()
move()
allowed = scan()
unlock(len(set(seen)))
say("Intruders:", sorted(set(seen) - set(allowed)))
say("Cleared:", sorted(set(seen) & set(allowed)))
while not at_exit():
    move()
x, y = position()
say("Out at x", x, "y", y)
hint: set(seen) - set(allowed) gives the intruders and & gives the cleared badges; wrap each in sorted() before saying it.

title: The filter press
story: At the Archive's exit sits the filter press, a machine that only accepts neatly processed data. Terminal 1 spits out raw numbers, terminal 2 a pile of crate labels typed in every possible case. The door code is the sum of the squares of the even numbers, and the press wants a clean index of the labels before it lets Bit through.
power: You often build a new collection from an old one. A comprehension does that in one readable line, instead of the empty-list, loop and append pattern. ### From a loop to a list comprehension A list comprehension is written in square brackets: first the expression that makes each new item, then a for part saying where the items come from. ~~~python doubled = [] for n in [1, 2, 3]: doubled.append(n * 2) print(doubled) doubled2 = [n * 2 for n in [1, 2, 3]] print(doubled2) ~~~ - Lines 1 to 3: the classic way gives [2, 4, 6]. - Line 6: read it as "n * 2, for each n in the list". Python loops for you and collects every result into a new list. ### Using range and list() Comprehensions work with any collection, including range. list(range(1, 6)) turns a range into a real list, which is handy to see its content. ~~~python nums = list(range(1, 6)) print(nums) squares = [n * n for n in nums] print(squares) ~~~ - Line 1: nums gets [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. - Line 3: squares gets [1, 4, 9, 16, 25]. ### Adding a filter with if Put an if at the end: only the items for which the condition is true are used. Read it as "expression, for each item, if condition". The filter is tested first, then the expression is computed for the items that passed. ~~~python nums = list(range(1, 11)) small = [n for n in nums if n < 4] odds = [n for n in nums if n % 2 == 1] tens = [n * 10 for n in nums if n % 3 == 0] print(small) print(odds) print(tens) ~~~ - Line 2: [1, 2, 3]. - Line 3: n % 2 == 1 is true for odd numbers: [1, 3, 5, 7, 9]. Even numbers are n % 2 == 0. - Line 4: first keeps 3, 6 and 9, then multiplies each by 10: [30, 60, 90]. ### Set comprehensions The same thing in curly braces gives a set, so duplicates disappear. ~~~python words = ["Gear", "gear", "BOLT", "bolt"] lowered = {w.lower() for w in words} print(sorted(lowered)) ~~~ - Line 2: w.lower() gives "gear" twice and "bolt" twice; the set keeps each once. - Line 3: prints ['bolt', 'gear']. ### Dict comprehensions With curly braces and a key: value expression, you get a dict. Each item from the loop produces one pair. Any function can be used in the value part, for example len(c) for the number of characters. ~~~python prices = [10, 25, 40] with_tax = {p: p * 1.2 for p in prices} print(with_tax) cities = ["Paris", "Nice"] print({c: c[0] for c in cities}) print({c: len(c) for c in cities}) ~~~ - Line 3: prints {10: 12.0, 25: 30.0, 40: 48.0}. - Line 5: prints {'Paris': 'P', 'Nice': 'N'}. - Line 6: prints {'Paris': 5, 'Nice': 4}. ### Common mistakes - Putting the if before the for: [n if n > 2 for n in nums] is a SyntaxError. The filter goes at the end. - Forgetting the colon in a dict comprehension: {c, len(c) for c in cities} is not valid. - Using square brackets when a dict is wanted: square brackets always build a list. - Writing n % 2 when you mean even numbers: that is true for odd ones.
goal: Scan the numbers (terminal 1) and the labels (terminal 2). With comprehensions, build even_squares (the squares of the even numbers, in order), tags (a set of the labels in lowercase) and lengths (a dict from each tag, in sorted order, to its length). Unlock door A with the sum of even_squares, reach the exit, then say Tags: with the sorted tags, and say lengths.
starter:
from robot import *

move()
nums = scan()
move()
move()
labels = scan()
solution:
from robot import *

move()
nums = scan()
move()
move()
labels = scan()
even_squares = [n * n for n in nums if n % 2 == 0]
tags = {w.lower() for w in labels}
lengths = {t: len(t) for t in sorted(tags)}
unlock(sum(even_squares))
move()
move()
say("Tags:", sorted(tags))
say(lengths)
hint: [n * n for n in nums if n % 2 == 0], then {w.lower() for w in labels}, then {t: len(t) for t in sorted(tags)}.
test:
assert isinstance(even_squares, list), 'even_squares must be a list (square brackets).'
assert isinstance(tags, set), 'tags must be a set (curly braces, no colon).'
assert isinstance(lengths, dict), 'lengths must be a dict (curly braces with key: value).'

title: Reusable moves
story: Bit rolls onto the Assembly Line: long belts, dead-end bays and the same moves over and over. Typing move() twenty times is how robots get stuck here. A terminal says how far the spare battery coin lies behind Bit and how far the exit lies ahead. Time to teach Bit new moves of its own.
power: A function is a named block of code you can run again and again just by writing its name. You have used many already: print, len, move. Now you write your own. ### Defining and calling a function You create a function with the keyword def (short for define), then a name, then round brackets, then a colon. The indented lines below form the function's body. Defining a function does not run it. The body runs only when you call the function, by writing its name followed by brackets. ~~~python def beep_twice(): print("Beep!") print("Beep!") print("Before the call") beep_twice() beep_twice() ~~~ - Line 1: def creates a function called beep_twice. The empty brackets mean it needs no information. Nothing is printed yet. - Lines 2 and 3: the body, indented by 4 spaces. Python stores these lines for later. - Line 4: back at the left edge, so this line is outside the function. It runs now. - Line 5: calls the function. Python jumps into the body, prints its two lines, then comes back here. - Line 6: calls it again, so two more beeps. ### Parameters and arguments The names inside the brackets of the def line are parameters: empty slots. The values you write in the brackets when you call the function are arguments: they fill the slots, in order. A function can call other functions, including ones you wrote. ~~~python def step(n): for i in range(n): print("step", i + 1, "of", n) def patrol(out, back): step(out) print("turning around") step(back) patrol(2, 3) ~~~ - Line 1: step has one parameter, n. - Line 5: inside patrol, the call step(out) fills n with the value of out. - Line 8: out is 2 and back is 3, so it prints 2 steps, the turn, then 3 steps. ### Variables inside a function A variable created inside a function, like i above, only exists while that call runs. Each call gets its own fresh copies, and the code outside cannot see them. This keeps functions from stepping on each other. ~~~python def make_label(part): label = part.upper() + "-01" return label print(make_label("gear")) print(make_label("nut")) ~~~ - Line 2: label lives only inside the function. - Line 3: return sends the value back to the caller (more on that in the next mission). - Lines 4 and 5: print GEAR-01 and NUT-01. Writing print(label) at the bottom would fail: there is no label outside. ### Common mistakes - Forgetting the colon after def name(...), or forgetting to indent the body. - Defining a function and never calling it: nothing happens. - Forgetting the brackets when calling: beep_twice alone names the function but does not run it.
goal: Write a function turn_around() (two left turns) and a function walk(n) that moves n squares. Walk onto the terminal, scan the two distances [behind, ahead] (from the terminal to the coin, and from the terminal to the exit), fetch the coin, then turn around and walk to the exit.
starter:
from robot import *

def turn_around():
    # two turns
    pass
solution:
from robot import *

def turn_around():
    turn_left()
    turn_left()
def walk(n):
    for i in range(n):
        move()
walk(1)
behind, ahead = scan()
walk(behind)
pick()
turn_around()
walk(behind + ahead)
hint: walk(n) is a for loop over range(n) with move() inside; after pick(), Bit must walk back past the terminal: behind + ahead squares.
test:
assert 'walk' in dir() and callable(walk), 'Write a function called walk(n).'
assert 'turn_around' in dir() and callable(turn_around), 'Write a function called turn_around().'
from robot import facing as _facing
_d = _facing()
turn_around()
assert _facing() == {'N': 'S', 'S': 'N', 'E': 'W', 'W': 'E'}[_d], 'turn_around() must leave Bit facing the opposite way.'
turn_around()

title: The pressure gauges
story: The belts are driven by steam, and the gauge terminal shows the pressure of every press. Bit must call out each one as low, ok or high before the foreman's ghost of a log will accept it. Door A opens with the total pressure, and door B, WARDEN's little joke, with the total plus 7.
power: ### return: sending a value back The keyword return ends the function and sends a value back to the place where it was called. A call can then be used anywhere a value can: stored, printed, added. ~~~python def area(width, height): result = width * height return result small = area(3, 4) print(small) print(area(10, 2) + 1) ~~~ - Line 4: the arguments fill the slots: width is 3 and height is 4. The call returns 12, stored in small. - Line 6: area(10, 2) becomes 20, then 20 + 1 is printed: 21. ### Printing is not returning print() only shows a value on the screen: the caller gets nothing back. A function that ends without return gives back the special value None, which means "no value". ~~~python def show_double(n): print(n * 2) def give_double(n): return n * 2 a = show_double(5) b = give_double(5) print(a, b) ~~~ - Line 5: prints 10 on the screen, but there is no return, so a gets None. - Line 6: nothing is printed; b gets 10. - Line 7: prints None 10. Only a returned value can be reused by other code, and the mission checks your functions by what they return. ### Default values and keyword arguments A parameter can have a default value, written name=value in the def line. If the caller leaves that argument out, the default is used. When calling, you can also name the arguments, like punctuation="!". These are keyword arguments, and their order no longer matters. Parameters with a default must come after the ones without. ~~~python def welcome(name, punctuation="."): return f"Welcome, {name}{punctuation}" print(welcome("Ada")) print(welcome("Bo", "!")) print(welcome(punctuation="?", name="Cy")) ~~~ - Line 3: punctuation uses its default: Welcome, Ada. - Line 4: the second argument replaces the default: Welcome, Bo! - Line 5: keyword arguments, in any order: Welcome, Cy? ### Returning early from an if chain A function can contain several return lines. The first one reached ends the function. So an if / elif chain can return a different answer for each range, and a last return catches everything left over. Functions can also use the result of other functions. ~~~python def speed_label(kmh): if kmh < 30: return "slow" elif kmh < 90: return "normal" return "fast" def to_kmh(meters, seconds): return round(meters / seconds * 3.6, 1) s = to_kmh(500, 20) print(s, speed_label(s)) print(speed_label(29.9), speed_label(30)) ~~~ - Lines 1 to 6: below 30 returns "slow" and stops right there. Otherwise, below 90 returns "normal". If neither matched, the last line returns "fast". No else is needed. - Line 9: 500 / 20 is 25.0, times 3.6 is 90.0. - Line 10: prints 90.0 fast, because 90 is not below 90. - Line 11: slow normal: watch where the boundary values land. Reminder: ** raises to a power, so x ** 2 is x squared, and it is computed before / and *. ### Common mistakes - Using print instead of return: the value shows on screen, but your function returns None. - Testing ranges in a jumbled order. Start from the smallest threshold with <, so each branch only sees what is left. - Putting a parameter with a default before one without: def f(a=1, b) is a SyntaxError.
goal: Write status(p) returning "low" below 30, "ok" below 70 and "high" otherwise, and code_for(readings, shift=0) returning the sum of the readings plus shift. Scan the gauges, say each reading and its status (like 45 ok), unlock door A with code_for(readings) and door B with code_for(readings, shift=7), then reach the exit.
starter:
from robot import *

def status(p):
    # return "low", "ok" or "high"
    pass
solution:
from robot import *

def status(p):
    if p < 30:
        return "low"
    elif p < 70:
        return "ok"
    return "high"
def code_for(readings, shift=0):
    return sum(readings) + shift
move()
readings = scan()
for p in readings:
    say(p, status(p))
unlock(code_for(readings))
move()
move()
unlock(code_for(readings, shift=7))
move()
move()
hint: status is an if / elif chain that returns early; code_for has the default shift=0 in its def line.
test:
assert 'status' in dir() and 'code_for' in dir(), 'Write the functions status(p) and code_for(readings, shift=0).'
assert status(29.9) == 'low' and status(30) == 'ok' and status(69) == 'ok' and status(70) == 'high', 'status must return (not print) low below 30, ok below 70, high otherwise.'
assert code_for([1, 2, 3]) == 6, 'code_for([1, 2, 3]) should return 6: shift defaults to 0.'
assert code_for([1, 2], shift=5) == 8, 'code_for([1, 2], shift=5) should return 8.'

title: The crate stamper
story: Crates roll past in threes, and the scale terminal gives their weights. The loading door opens for the total weight. Then the stamping machine wants a label for the batch, written as tidy name=value pairs in alphabetical order, or it jams the whole line.
power: Sometimes you cannot know in advance how many values a function will receive. Python has special parameters for that. ### *args: any number of positional arguments A parameter written with one star, like *args, collects all the positional arguments (the ones without a name) into a tuple. The name after the star is up to you; args is just the usual choice. ~~~python def show(*items): print(items) print(len(items), "item(s)") show("a", "b", "c") show(42) show() ~~~ - Line 4: items is ('a', 'b', 'c') and the count is 3. - Line 5: one argument gives a one-item tuple, shown as (42,). The comma marks it as a tuple. - Line 6: no arguments gives an empty tuple () and a count of 0. ### Using the collected values A tuple works with everything you used on lists: for loops, len(), max(), min(), and sum(), which gives 0 for an empty collection. ~~~python def average(*scores): if len(scores) == 0: return 0 return sum(scores) / len(scores) print(average(12, 15, 18)) print(average()) print(sum((1, 2, 3)), sum(())) print(max((4, 9, 2)), min((4, 9, 2))) ~~~ - Lines 2 and 3: with no scores, return 0 early, because dividing by 0 would crash. - Line 5: 45 divided by 3: 15.0. - Line 6: 0. - Line 7: 6 0. Line 8: 9 2. ### **kwargs: any number of keyword arguments Two stars, like **kwargs, collect every keyword argument (name=value) into a dict. The names become the keys, as strings. ~~~python def profile(**info): print(info) for key, value in info.items(): print(key, "is", value) profile(name="Ada", city="London", age=36) ~~~ - Line 2: prints {'name': 'Ada', 'city': 'London', 'age': 36}. The keys keep the order you wrote them in. - Lines 3 and 4: one line per pair. ### Sorting keys and joining text sorted() on a dict gives a list of its keys in alphabetical order. "sep".join(list_of_strings) glues strings together with sep between them. With a list comprehension, they turn a dict into a tidy line of text. ~~~python def tags(**options): keys = sorted(options) print(keys) parts = [f"{k}:{options[k]}" for k in keys] print(parts) return " | ".join(parts) print(tags(size="L", color="red", qty=2)) ~~~ - Line 2: ['color', 'qty', 'size']. - Line 4: one string per key; the f-string turns the number 2 into text. - Line 6: returns color:red | qty:2 | size:L. Inside join() you may drop the square brackets: " | ".join(f"{k}:{options[k]}" for k in keys) gives the same result. Without brackets it is a generator expression: it hands the strings to join one by one instead of building a list first. Joining zero strings gives the empty text "". ### Common mistakes - Forgetting that *args is a tuple and **kwargs is a dict. - Forgetting the star in the def line: def total(nums) accepts exactly one argument. - Passing numbers to join: it only glues strings, so convert with an f-string or str().
goal: Write total(*weights) returning the sum of all its arguments, and stamp(**fields) returning the key=value pairs in sorted key order, joined by ", ". Scan the three weights (terminal 1) and the destination (terminal 2), unlock door A with the total weight, reach the exit, then say stamp(weight=..., dest=..., crates=3) with the total and the destination.
solution:
from robot import *

def total(*weights):
    return sum(weights)
def stamp(**fields):
    return ", ".join(f"{k}={fields[k]}" for k in sorted(fields))
move()
a, b, c = scan()
move()
move()
dest = scan()
unlock(total(a, b, c))
move()
move()
say(stamp(weight=total(a, b, c), dest=dest, crates=3))
hint: ", ".join(f"{k}={fields[k]}" for k in sorted(fields)) builds the stamp.
test:
assert 'total' in dir() and 'stamp' in dir(), 'Write the functions total(*weights) and stamp(**fields).'
assert total() == 0 and total(5) == 5 and total(1, 2, 3, 4) == 10, 'total must return the sum of any number of arguments (0 for none).'
assert stamp(b=2, a=1) == 'a=1, b=2', 'stamp(b=2, a=1) should return "a=1, b=2".'
assert stamp() == '', 'stamp() with no fields should return an empty text.'

title: The sorting belt
story: The sorting belt has stopped with a pile of crates on it, each one a pair of a name and a weight. It restarts only when Bit reads them out from lightest to heaviest. Door A answers to the name of the heaviest crate, door B to the name of the lightest.
power: ### lambda: a tiny function in one line lambda creates a small function without a name: lambda parameters: expression. It returns the value of the expression automatically, with no return keyword. It is handy when you need a function only once. ~~~python square = lambda n: n * n def square_def(n): return n * n print(square(4), square_def(4)) ~~~ - Line 1: a function that takes n and gives back n * n, stored in square. - Lines 2 and 3: the very same function written with def. - Line 4: prints 16 16. ### key=: telling sorted, max and min what to compare sorted(), max() and min() accept a key= argument: a function applied to each item to get the value to compare. The items themselves come back unchanged. A lambda is the usual way to write that function. Add reverse=True to sorted() to get the largest first. ~~~python products = [("pen", 1.5), ("bag", 25.0), ("mug", 8.0)] by_price = sorted(products, key=lambda p: p[1]) print(by_price) print(sorted(["kiwi", "fig", "banana"], key=len)) print(max(products, key=lambda p: p[1])) print(min(products, key=lambda p: p[1])[0]) print(sorted(products, key=lambda p: p[1], reverse=True)[0]) ~~~ - Line 2: for each tuple p, the key is p[1], its price. - Line 3: prints [('pen', 1.5), ('mug', 8.0), ('bag', 25.0)]. - Line 4: key=len passes the built-in len function itself (no brackets): ['fig', 'kiwi', 'banana']. - Line 5: the tuple with the highest price: ('bag', 25.0). - Line 6: the cheapest tuple, then [0] takes its name: pen. - Line 7: largest first, so ('bag', 25.0). ### Unpacking pairs in a loop When every item is a pair, a for loop can unpack it into two names, just like .items() on a dict. ~~~python crates = [["cog", 12], ["anvil", 80]] for name, weight in crates: print(name, "weighs", weight) ~~~ ### Common mistakes - Writing key=len() with brackets: that calls len right away. Pass the function itself. - Calling sorted() on pairs without key=: pairs are compared by their first item, here the name, so you get alphabetical order. - Forgetting that max with a key= returns the whole item, not the compared value.
goal: Scan the crates. Build by_weight, the crates sorted from lightest to heaviest with key= and a lambda, and say each name and weight (like cog 12) in that order. Unlock door A with the name of the heaviest crate and door B with the name of the lightest, then reach the exit.
starter:
from robot import *

move()
crates = scan()
solution:
from robot import *

move()
crates = scan()
by_weight = sorted(crates, key=lambda c: c[1])
for name, weight in by_weight:
    say(name, weight)
unlock(max(crates, key=lambda c: c[1])[0])
move()
move()
unlock(min(crates, key=lambda c: c[1])[0])
move()
move()
hint: key=lambda c: c[1] compares the weights; max(...)[0] is the name of the heaviest crate.
test:
assert 'by_weight' in dir() and isinstance(by_weight, list), 'Build the list by_weight with sorted().'
assert [c[1] for c in by_weight] == sorted(c[1] for c in by_weight), 'by_weight must go from the lightest crate to the heaviest.'

title: The recursive stairwell
story: At the end of the line, a stairwell climbs toward the upper floors. Every step looks exactly like the one before it, and the terminal at the bottom says how many there are. At the top, door A wants the factorial of that number: WARDEN likes big numbers.
power: Recursion is when a function calls itself. It is the natural way to handle problems that contain smaller copies of themselves: a stairwell of n steps is one step, then a stairwell of n - 1 steps. ### A function that calls itself Every recursive function needs two parts. A base case: a situation simple enough to answer directly, which stops the calls. And a recursive case: the function calls itself on a smaller problem, getting one step closer to the base case each time. ~~~python def countdown(n): if n == 0: print("Go!") return print(n) countdown(n - 1) countdown(3) ~~~ - Lines 2 to 4: the base case. When n is 0, print Go! and stop. A bare return just ends the function. - Line 5: otherwise, print the current number. - Line 6: the recursive case: call countdown again with a number one smaller. - Line 7: countdown(3) prints 3 and calls countdown(2), which prints 2 and calls countdown(1), which prints 1 and calls countdown(0), which prints Go!. Each call has its own private n. Use Step through to watch four separate calls, each with its own value. ### Returning values from recursive calls Recursion gets powerful when each call returns a value that the call before it uses. The sum 1 + 2 + ... + n is n plus the sum up to n - 1, and the sum up to 0 is 0. ~~~python def sum_to(n): if n == 0: return 0 return n + sum_to(n - 1) print(sum_to(3)) print(sum_to(10)) ~~~ - Line 4: Python must finish sum_to(n - 1) before it can do the addition. - Line 5: sum_to(3) waits for sum_to(2), which waits for sum_to(1), which waits for sum_to(0). That one returns 0. Then the waiting calls finish in reverse order: 1 + 0 = 1, then 2 + 1 = 3, then 3 + 3 = 6. Prints 6. - Line 6: prints 55. The same shape with multiplication gives the factorial: the factorial of 5 is 5 x 4 x 3 x 2 x 1 = 120. Think about what the base case must return for a product: a number that changes nothing when you multiply by it. The factorial of 0 is 1. ### What happens without a base case If the function never reaches a base case, it keeps calling itself until Python gives up: ~~~text RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded ~~~ Make sure every call moves toward the base case, for example with n - 1, never n itself. ### Common mistakes - No base case, or a call that does not get smaller: RecursionError. - Forgetting to return the result of the recursive call, so the answer is lost on the way back. - A wrong base value: 0 is right for a sum, but would turn every product into 0.
goal: Write a recursive climb(n): with 0 steps left, say Top; otherwise say n, climb one step (forward, turn left, forward, turn right) and call climb(n - 1). Write a recursive factorial(n). Scan the number of steps, climb, then unlock door A with the factorial of that number and step onto the exit.
solution:
from robot import *

def climb(n):
    if n == 0:
        say("Top")
        return
    say(n)
    move()
    turn_left()
    move()
    turn_right()
    climb(n - 1)
def factorial(n):
    if n == 0:
        return 1
    return n * factorial(n - 1)
move()
n = scan()
climb(n)
unlock(factorial(n))
move()
move()
hint: factorial has the same shape as sum_to, with * instead of + and a base case that returns 1.
test:
assert 'climb' in dir() and 'factorial' in dir(), 'Write the functions climb(n) and factorial(n).'
assert factorial(0) == 1 and factorial(5) == 120, 'factorial(0) must be 1 and factorial(5) must be 120.'
_f = factorial
globals()['factorial'] = lambda n: -1000
_r = _f(3)
globals()['factorial'] = _f
assert _r != 6, 'factorial must call itself (recursion), not use a loop.'
_keep = {k: globals()[k] for k in ('move', 'turn_left', 'turn_right', 'say', 'climb')}
_calls = []
globals()['move'] = lambda: None
globals()['turn_left'] = lambda: None
globals()['turn_right'] = lambda: None
globals()['say'] = lambda *a: None
globals()['climb'] = lambda n: _calls.append(n)
_keep['climb'](2)
globals().update(_keep)
assert _calls == [1], 'climb(n) must call climb(n - 1) itself: no loops, recursion.'

title: Crates inside crates
story: The last gate of the Assembly Line is a row of doors, and WARDEN hid their codes in a shipping manifest of crates packed inside crates inside crates. Nobody knows how deep the packing goes. Bit needs one flat list of codes, in order, to open the doors one after another.
power: To walk through lists inside lists, a function must decide for each item: is it a list (go deeper, with a recursive call) or a plain value? ### isinstance: what kind of value is this? isinstance(value, type) returns True if the value is of that type, otherwise False. list is the type of lists, str the type of text, int the type of whole numbers. ~~~python print(isinstance([1, 2], list)) print(isinstance(7, list)) print(isinstance("hi", str)) print(isinstance(7, int)) ~~~ - Prints True, False, True, True. ### append versus extend append(x) adds x as one single item, even if x is itself a list. extend(other_list) adds each item of other_list separately. ~~~python a = [1, 2] a.append([3, 4]) print(a) b = [1, 2] b.extend([3, 4]) print(b) ~~~ - Line 3: prints [1, 2, [3, 4]]: the whole list became one item. - Line 6: prints [1, 2, 3, 4]. ### Recursion on nested lists This function counts every plain value in a list, however deeply nested. For each item: if it is a list, ask the same function to count inside it; otherwise count 1. ~~~python def count_values(items): total = 0 for item in items: if isinstance(item, list): total += count_values(item) else: total += 1 return total print(count_values([1, 2, 3])) print(count_values([1, [2, [3, 4]], 5])) print(count_values([[], [[]]])) ~~~ - Line 2: each call starts its own counter at 0. - Lines 4 and 5: a sub-list is handled by a recursive call, and the count it returns is added to total. - Line 10: the outer call counts 1, then calls itself on [2, [3, 4]]. That call counts 2 and calls itself on [3, 4], which returns 2, so the middle call returns 3. Back at the top: 1 + 3 + 1 = 5. - Line 11: empty lists contain no values: 0. The base case is hidden here: a list with no sub-lists makes no further calls. To build a flat list instead of a count, start from an empty list instead of 0, and pick the right list method in each branch. ### Common mistakes - Using append where you meant extend, which puts a whole list inside your list. - Forgetting to return the result at the end, so every caller gets None. - Starting the result list outside the function: all the calls would share it.
goal: Write a recursive flatten(items) that turns any nested list into one flat list, keeping the order. Scan the manifest, flatten it, say Codes found: and how many codes there are, unlock each door in turn with the next code, and reach the exit.
starter:
from robot import *

def flatten(items):
    flat = []
    return flat
hint: For each item: if isinstance(item, list), extend the result with flatten(item), otherwise append the item.
test:
assert 'flatten' in dir(), 'Write a function called flatten(items).'
assert flatten([1, [2, [3, []]], 4]) == [1, 2, 3, 4], 'flatten([1, [2, [3, []]], 4]) should return [1, 2, 3, 4].'
assert flatten([]) == [], 'flatten([]) should return [].'
_f = flatten
globals()['flatten'] = lambda items: ['deeper']
_r = _f([[1]])
globals()['flatten'] = _f
assert _r == ['deeper'], 'flatten must call itself on each sub-list (recursion).'
